utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it would be no protective measures, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's Mr. Milincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, it isn't, actually, Your Honours. It's Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm happy to say, I don't think there are any protective measures for Mr. Milincic either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I mixed up the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic is the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one small matter that I may raise at this opportunity. Mr. Harmon has discussed with Mr. Josse the stipulation to the positions of the gentleman Hadzo Efendic, which was the issue with the witness Stavnjak, and I'm informed that the Defence is willing to stipulate that he was appointed vice-president of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 25th of February, 1993, and he was also appointed to the position of ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Austria on the 4th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's then on the record, exact dates and positions: Vice-president of BiH, 25th of February, 1993; and ambassador of BH in Austria, 4th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Defence does agree with both those points, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the witness may be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Antic, if I'm right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Antic. You'll first be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Strictly, I think I'm going to leave the cross-examination to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll do it a milder way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Monday morning. I hope --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honour, since I'm doing what I'm doing, I was proposing to go fairly quickly through some of the early material and lead. Of course, if at any point the Prosecution feel I'm overstepping the mark, well, I'm confident they will say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were born on -- well, your name is Bozidar Antic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were born on the 25th of November, 1957, in Sarajevo, and you have a degree in economics from Sarajevo University; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were previously a member of the Communist Party, although you were never a very active member; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It is. I was a formal member, as most young people back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And up to 1990, and I'm really talking about time of the multi-party elections in November 1990, you lived in an apartment with your wife and then two very young children, in a part of Sarajevo called Dobrinja 5 and you worked in Kiseljak, which is also in the area of Sarajevo, as the general manager of a successful textile company called Globus. Is all that I've just said correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it right - and please correct if it isn't - that the ethnic composition of the population in Kiseljak was about 50 per cent Croats, about 40 to 45 per cent Muslims, and the balance were mainly Serbs, and then others, which means people who would describe themselves as Yugoslavs, for example? Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It is. The figures seem to be correct. At any rate, the majority population was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And very briefly, because you were there, how would you describe to the Trial Chamber that the Croats in Kiseljak conducted themselves on the local political level?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: You mean prior to the elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps I can just nudge it this way: Having regard to the fact that the Croats did constitute about 50 per cent, how did they conduct themselves in local politics in Kiseljak in the context of their having 50 per cent of the population?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can tell you very briefly that up until the multi-party elections, everything worked in more or less the same way as everywhere else in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was the so-called national key enshrined in the communist system, and up until then, everything worked as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did the -- from your observation, did the Croats give appropriate recognition and weight to the Muslim and Serb and other elements of the population in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I never noticed anything amiss during that time. Everything was more or less normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did that change in any noticeable way after the November 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I didn't get involved or know much about the internal power-sharing agreements at the municipal level, but a certain emotional charge could be felt, that is to say, the victory of the national parties, and you could see it everywhere, even though there were no visible problems of any sort, no tangible problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a specific effect on you personally of the outcome of the 1990 multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I never felt it until the point in time when I started being criticised by some parties, in terms of them claiming that I was unsuitable for the post that I held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you -- when you say you started being criticised by some parties, could you be as specific as you can about who it was that was criticising you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: First of all, HDZ, through the media and at press conferences that they had at the party level, at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there any individual in particular who, on behalf of the HDZ, was making that criticism of you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I remember the first meeting of the BH Presidency, the newly elected one, and Mr. Kljuic was present at that meeting, Stjepan Kljuic, who was the member of the BH Presidency, and he raised that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was his criticism of you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It was not really a direct reference to my name as such, but they kept saying that the new authorities would do all they can in order to put a stop to the misuse or abuse taking place within the framework of the privatisation process, and they quoted one example, and of course that was the example of my company, the company that I was the manager of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Globus was at that time undergoing, was it, or about to undergo, a process of privatisation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Globus went through the privatisation process, and it was one of the rare companies that went through this process with no intentions whatsoever, and everybody was satisfied at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Why did you, as it seems you did, why did you understand what was being said about the company, not naming you, as a criticism of you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, they kept referring to the management of the company, the manager, but they did not actually refer to my name as such, but it was an extremely veiled reference, I mean, and also it wasn't difficult for people to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you mean that it was an extremely veiled reference or that it was a thinly veiled reference?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Perhaps thinly veiled reference. It was clear to all who was meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was it that was being suggested as the misuse or abuse within the framework of the privatisation process?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The overall context of the discussion was about the new authorities putting a stop to any misuse of state property. No details were mentioned, but it was considered that the privatisation process at my company basically meant that shares went into my own pocket and the pockets of my friends. But it was not true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any pressure to -- of any sort to remove you from your post?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the local level, there were indirect suggestions to that effect, but to a considerable extent, there was also some protection of my person and my achievements, and there were very many Croats who actually resisted that pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's start, then: Who was -- well, when did the pressure to remove you from your post begin?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Straight after the election results were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was bringing that pressure?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned that. Officially, it was done within other statements for the press, for the media, within the framework of the HDZ for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and at that particular meeting of the Presidency, of the BH Presidency. And what happened on the ground was just a reflection of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it only the Croat leadership in the HDZ who criticised your company and you indirectly, or did anybody else also make such a criticism?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It was just the HDZ leadership at those press conferences, and at the Presidency meeting, the SDA leadership joined in, but probably out of some kind of solidarity. I mean, Alija Izetbegovic and -- they also said that any misuse of state property should be stopped or prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So who gave you support in your position in relation to that pressure?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, staff. Many employees signed a petition and they addressed it to the media and all the parties, saying that what was being done was unreasonable and based on lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you offered any support from outside the company?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a few people who individually lent me their support, and who came to me asking if I needed any assistance or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Apart from individual support, were you offered any support from within the Serb political community?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: After all that, since it was a hyped-up media event, as it were, for a certain period of time, I was invited to get in touch with the Serb Democratic Party, in case I felt it was necessary, and to give an account of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, can you remember who issued that invitation to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Some of my friends who were in closer contact with Dr. Karadzic, or at least who knew him, since I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you then establish or have some sort of contact in relation to this matter with Dr. Karadzic himself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I went to see him at his surgery in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able to put some sort of -- best you can do, some sort of date on that visit to Dr. Karadzic's surgery?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can't really recall the date after such a long time, but I think it was at some point in December, after the elections which took place by the end of November. So I think it was in December 1990, I suppose. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you met Dr. Karadzic personally? That's correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there anybody else from the Bosnian Serb leadership present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And keeping it reasonably briefly, please, Mr. Antic, what was the discussion -- I'm assuming there was some discussion; what was the discussion between you and Dr. Karadzic at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: We had a very brief discussion only and exclusively about my position back in Kiseljak, and I explained what the situation was and I explained who I was, what I did, why I did what I did, and why I was being attacked. And I convinced him -- or at least I tried to convince him that all those stories and rumours were totally untrue. Dr. Karadzic asked me, "Well, what do you expect me to do? How do you think I can help you? Would you like to stay at that company or would you like to leave or what?" And I said that I would perhaps only like him to try and talk to the HDZ people and that, for the time being, I preferred to stay on, and that I would wait and see and then maybe get in touch again in case there were any further problems. And I made my own private decision to stay a little while longer and then actually leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, at the end of that meeting, did you leave Dr. Karadzic with the understanding that you were going to try to stay at the company for the long run?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: That was a conclusion of some sort, but we, of course -- I didn't know for how long. My decision was to try and await the annual reports so that everybody could know what the state of the company was when I left and not for other people to be judges of that, through press conferences or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the end of the financial year for Globus was the 28th of February; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just jumping ahead for a moment on that: Did you in the end stay until just after the end of the financial year on the 28th of February, put through the accounts for that year, and then, very shortly after that date, leave the company?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I stayed on until the 28th of February. I presented the annual accounts. All that was approved, with a number of my staff I went out to lunch and we had a celebratory lunch, as it were, and a farewell one, and then I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Going back to your meeting with Dr. Karadzic, then, was there any discussion or suggestion at that meeting with Dr. Karadzic about your becoming politically involved with the Serb community or the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. We discussed my case, only my case, nothing else. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn whether or not the SDS leadership had in fact spoken to anybody to try to -- on your behalf in relation to Globus?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned subsequently and I felt that the pressure was subsiding. There were no longer attacks like at the beginning. But I was clear that it was time for me to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you -- did you learn who had spoken to whom to give you that support?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Rajko Dukic, the president of the Executive Board, I suppose, of the party, who was in charge of the inter-party staff issues, that's the person I met subsequently. He told me that he had spoken to Stjepan Kljuic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say Rajko Dukic, the president of the Executive Board of the party, just to make it absolutely clear for the record, that's the SDS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about his conversation or conversations with Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. He interpreted his conversation with Kljuic jokingly, and he said, when he asked them how come that you were attacking Antic, Kljuic answered, "The lad is good. There's nothing wrong with him. But is it normal for a Serb to be a director of a company in the town where Croats are a majority?" That was the only reason why I was attacked. No other issues were at stake, either privatisation or anything else; that was the only reason. I understood that as a joke, but unfortunately, something that was practiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you understand what you've just told the Trial Chamber to reflect some wider approach of Mr. Kljuic and his colleagues as opposed to just something directed against you and your company?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that as a wider approach. From the very beginning, I knew that it was not personal, I was just chosen as a good example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Example of what?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: They had to start with somebody on that road, and maybe the best example would have been Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say they had to start with somebody on that road. Can you perhaps help the Trial Chamber with what you mean by "that road"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I do not want to speculate, but the road was for the Croatian companies to be given to Croatian directors. I'm talking about the economy, the sphere of life where I spent most of my time. When they selected their Croatian directors, they could probably influence the life and the economy, which would not have been possible if that was not the case, which of course is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As you were continuing to work at the company up until the end of February 1991, as you describe, was there an issue relating to your apartment that you needed to resolve?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Nobody raised that issue particularly, but there was a law in place which said that if you were to acquire tenancy rights, you had to spend ten years in a company. At that time I had been with the company nine years and a half. I was six months short and I -- there was a risk that I might lose my tenancy right. Nobody actually mentioned that, but I had that in mind and I went to the Municipal Assembly of Ilidza to try and iron out, so to speak, those six months and secure the tenancy rights for me, for the apartment where I was residing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you get it sorted out satisfactorily?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the Municipal Assembly of Ilidza --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about the details, Mr. Antic. If the answer is yes, you've got it --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I sorted it out. Yes, you're right. I got it sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ask for or receive any help from anybody in the SDS in sorting out that issue about your apartment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need for that. This was a legal matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the -- anybody in the SDS even know that you had this problem to sort out and that you were sorting it out?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the -- anybody in the SDS know before you left the company at the end of February that that was the date when you were leaving and that was the date that you left?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. No. That was my personal decision and that was my personal plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have -- your staying in the company until the 28th of February to get the accounts done for that year, was that based on any underlying concerns about your own personal position?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. My conscience was clear. The company was in good shape. Everybody was happy. I had a fantastic relationship with everybody there at the time, and later on, so I only wanted to withdraw honourably from that position and not to have my name smeared in any way after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I take it that you've finished with the apartment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question. The Ilidza Municipal Assembly, was there any party with a majority? Could you give us an idea on how Croats, Muslims, Serbs, were represented in that Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croats had a minority there. I don't know the percentage. And the Serbs and the Muslims had a very close percentage, very -- almost equal percentage. I don't know how much again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who replaced you when -- at Globus when you left?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I was replaced by my former assistant for finances, Mehmed Lujinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he was a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason that you were -- well, he was your deputy, we can see that. But was there any particular reason why he got the job?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The only reason was the fact that the people from the company managed to elect him internally as somebody who was familiar with the job. They did not want anybody, be it a Croat or a Muslim, who was not familiar with the job. So people from the company managed to win the battle with the politics and managed to have their own person elected, because he knew the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you still have relations and contacts with former colleagues at Globus from that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We have remained in very good relations, and I can say that when I was with that company, this was one of the best periods of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the next bit, Mr. Antic, I'm going to put a number of points to you, so if you'd just listen carefully and then tell the Trial Chamber whether you can confirm what I'm saying to you. Is this right: You then went to work in Ilidza, which is a separate municipality from Kiseljak, you went to Ilidza at the invitation of the local political leadership there, where you became minister for commerce or business; you started your own business there in Ilidza straight away, with two partners, in the manufacture and retail of clothing; your business was called Nikola's and it now is, but largely in Belgrade as a development, it is now a very successful business; you have 24 retail outlets in Belgrade and it is a flourishing concern stemming from that business you started in 1991; that a number of employees came from Globus, which was in the textile business, to work for you in Ilidza, especially those, not surprisingly, who lived nearer to Ilidza; most of them were Muslims, but they also included some Serbs and possibly a small number of Croats; and that you yourself had no particular problems with any of those workers from any ethnic group; and at the time that you moved to Ilidza, you remained throughout living in the apartment in Dobrinja 5. That's quite a long chunk. Please say if you've got any doubts about that. But are you able to confirm the correctness of everything that I have just put to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Everything is correct. I would only say that this was not a concern; it was a private company. It was not a conglomerate of companies, it was just a private company. Everything else is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Just to clarify that: What I was intending to put to you or what was implicit, of course it started off in 1991 in Ilidza and you're saying, are you, it started off, of course, as a small concern; it's become, over more than a decade, it's now become - but moved to Belgrade - a very large concern; correct? Not a multinational, but a large, thriving business; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it was early March 1991 when you moved to work in Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you receive any approach or contact after you moved to Ilidza from the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. After maybe a month or a month and a half, I was invited from the office of Dr. Karadzic. I got in contact with him because he did not know that I had already come to Ilidza. He asked me to come and have a conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you take up his invitation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where did you go -- you went to see him, did you, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, it was in the same place; in his surgery, in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you went to see him, are we in April 1991 or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you went to see Dr. Karadzic, was there any other member of the SDS leadership present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, as briefly, but so the Trial Chamber can fully understand what happened, what was the discussion between you and Dr. Karadzic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic didn't know that I had left the company. He was familiar with the case, though. He learnt that and he told me that his thought about my engagement in the municipality was beyond my capabilities -- below my capabilities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he asked me if I would fill a ministerial place, as there was an opening on the SDS quota, and he asked me if I would consider that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And to clarify, not that I believe it's any great mystery, but just to make it clear for all concerned: We're talking about the Bosnia and Herzegovina government, of course, at this time, and when you refer to the quota, you're referring to something which is a reflection of the power-sharing agreements at a national level; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So did he offer you a specific ministerial position?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a minister without a portfolio, in the BiH government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was your response, Mr. Antic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: My response was that I would give it some thought and that I would get back to him. And I also told him that I would rather go into private business and that any solution that would exclude my own private business would not be acceptable for me. So I told him that if I could run my private business in parallel with that position that he was offering, then I would give it a serious thought. If that was not possible, then I wouldn't even think about it. And then Dr. Karadzic told me that it would be possible and that if I decided to accept his proposal and that if I realised that it was not possible for me to be a minister and to control my private business, that I should then resign, that it is only -- it was only fair for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And by the time you left that meeting on that day, what was your own personal thinking? Were you steering towards the positive on accepting this position or the other direction? Where were you on the spectrum yourself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I was rather surprised by that invitation, because I had not participated in all those things, and that's why I was surprised. I needed time to talk to my friends, to my family, and to talk to myself, actually, whether to accept that position or not. I was in two minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Dr. Karadzic explore in that discussion with you your own political views?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. We did not discuss that. He just offered me the position and he wanted to hear my response. That's all we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would he have been aware of your broad political views without needing to ask you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He may have been. I suppose so. I don't know. I can't give you a precise answer as to what he did know, what he didn't know. In any case, we never discussed that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, at this time, it's correct, is it: You were not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you ever been asked to join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Anyway, you did think it over and you did accept the position, and that was confirmed and you did become a member of the Bosnia and Herzegovina government; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you -- in fact, that happened, you joined the government around April 1991, did you, or very shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Thereabouts. April or maybe even May, but it will sooner be April than May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct that you had two particular -- almost straight away you were given two particular formal tasks or positions. One was as - and of course I'm giving it to you in English, so I hope it gets -- ends up in Serbian as something near to the original - as president of the Disaster Relief Agency, and also as the chairman or president of what is aptly described as the National Parole Board? Say if you're not comfortable with those descriptions as they're coming across to you, but does that sound -- is that right, Mr. Antic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: You put it really well. Both descriptions are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I take compliments when they're offered, Mr. Antic. Thank you. You remained in those positions until April 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That government, of course, consisted of, naturally, as you've indicated, and the Trial Chamber is well aware of this, Muslims and Croats and, like yourself, Serbs. How would you describe the contribution made by the Croat members of the government to the business and meetings and decisions of the Bosnia and Herzegovina government during the period of your membership?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the Croat members only?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was taking the -- asking you specifically first about - I'm going to come to others - specifically about the Croat members first, yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In general terms, I would say that the impression was that they tried to minimise the importance of the rest of Yugoslavia and its importance, and all the federal functions that concerned Bosnia and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Herzegovina, and especially the army. As with other issues, there were no problems, with the so-called regular issues. Whatever concerned the federal level, they tried to minimise it, they tried to deny the importance of those things, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What about the -- equivalent question: What about the contribution made by the Muslim members of the government to the business and meetings and decisions of the government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Initially, their contribution was more or less correct, because this was the period where solutions were sought for the remnants of the so-called functional federation, and there were no major problems. It was only towards the end of the year that similar things appeared with Muslims as had existed from the very beginning with the Croat members of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, was there, from your observations, was there a difference in the level of ability and experience as between the Serb, Croat, and Muslim elements of the government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It's very hard to say that for anybody. My impression was that most of the members of the government were completely anonymous and unknown by the general public, especially when we're talking about the Muslim members of the government, whereas the Serbian representatives were more or less generally and widely known, people who were familiar to the general public by their positions, by their views. But it's very difficult to accept that as a general statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From your membership with the government during that year, from April 1991 to 1992, did that government have -- well, what was the degree of influence that the government had on political events in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I mean, purely political events in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm not going to say that the government had no influence whatsoever, but no influence to speak of. Because whatever happened in politics happened at the level of the Presidency and within the parties and amongst the parties that met and negotiated things quite outside the realm of the government. And as to the government, they were just acting in a purely formal manner, in order to appear to be acting in line with the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does that mean that in your case, Mr. Antic - please try and make this clear to the Trial Chamber - are you saying you didn't really do anything or achieve anything as a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, you asked about political affairs. Yes, we did talk about other things, but as to political issues, very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's a difficult one, perhaps, Mr. Antic, but perhaps I should make it clear that for these purposes I would like you to take the word "political" in the broadest sense, to include all aspects of government, the economy, and so on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the question in relation at the moment to your own work over that year. Did you do much? Did you achieve much?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I was minister without a portfolio, so I did not have a ministry of my own, so I couldn't assess or measure the results of such a ministry, since it didn't exist. Of course, the participation in those committees was done properly and I tended to deal with issues having to do with the economy. It was what I knew best. And I did what I could. But I thought when you mentioned politics, that you meant party relations and inter-ethnic relations, and when I replied to your previous question, what I meant to say, that they -- the government, that is, could not influence that. And so, well, all things considered, there were no major results.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the economics minister a Muslim throughout your membership with the government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was any request - request or instruction, try to make it clear in your answer - given to you by the SDS as to where you should concentrate your work and your activities as a minister without portfolio?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously, as a minister without portfolio, I participated in work on almost all topics, but I was expected to do a little bit more with regard to anything to do with the economy. And those were the only additional instructions from the very start. From where I stood, it was only natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you -- all this time you were also running your business, you had an office somewhere, you worked in Ilidza; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You had an office as a minister without portfolio in the government building in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The SDS leadership were not in the same building as you and your office in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct; no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where was Mr. Krajisnik's office in relation to yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: At the building of the BH Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was a separate building, a different building entirely from where you had your office, was it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's the same group of buildings. They were all close together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik ever attend any government meetings during that year of your membership of the BiH government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Never, as far as I recall. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During that year - let's leave aside the two meetings that you've already told the Trial Chamber about with Dr. Karadzic before you became a minister - after you became a minister, did you have any further private or nearly private meetings with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever have any small meetings with Dr. Karadzic and a group, by which I mean fewer than ten people present?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think I was ever present at those really restricted meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you attend -- now, there was a building which was generally described as the SDS Deputies Club as a description of the building, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Deputies Club building. I think that was the name the building had even before the SDS. And that's what it used to be called. But it wasn't like MPs or something, nothing like that. It was just called the Deputies Club, and that's where these SDS meetings were held on occasion, on certain issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The reason I asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Terribly sorry to interrupt you. At this point in time of this hearing, I would like to know what vision did the witness have of this political situation, the global political situation, at that particular time? So he was a businessman, he then steps into the government, he is within the government, and while he is exercising a role within the government, he's also a businessman. But I would like to know, as a citizen, as an active citizen in those two fields, what was his point of view with regards to the general situation? What were the problems in the country at that time? How did he see those problems at the time? And I'm terribly sorry to continue, but he told us that within that government, there were no debates on political topics, or at least while he was present nothing was debated of the sort. But so what was his personal opinion of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to my own personal opinion, the situation was rather complex and vague, and I suppose, if I may put it in this way, that everybody was buying time somehow, until a final, overall solution was brought about by the international community with regard to the entire Yugoslav issue. So basically, everybody in Bosnia and Herzegovina was biding time and waiting to see what was going to happen. So there wasn't a huge chance of anything being resolved or settled independently at the Bosnia and Herzegovina level. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one additional question as well, Mr. Stewart. I'll let you finish -- I did let you finish your first portion, not to interfere unnecessarily. You said -- you were asked by Mr. Stewart when you took up your position as minister without portfolio, whether you were given by the SDS instructions as to where you should concentrate your work, and you said: "Well, as a minister without portfolio, I participated in work on almost all topics, but I was expected to do a little bit more with regard to anything to do with the economy and those were the only additional instructions from the very start." From whom did you receive those instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, back then, when I talked to Karadzic, it was at his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You received -- to focus on economical matters as an instruction from Mr. Karadzic. Yes. Your answer, now I understand, are instructions from Mr. Karadzic. The question was about instructions from the SDS. Was that the same to you, or ...? You understand, Mr. Karadzic could just speak on his own or as someone presenting the views of the SDS. What was the case, as far as you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understood that to be an instruction on behalf of the SDS. That's what he was at the time, the president of the SDS. And that was sufficient. That's how I saw it, as the instructions coming from the party at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he have any official government position at that time, Mr. Karadzic, when he asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was just the party chairman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, so far as the Deputies Club was concerned, what I was trying to do, so there was no misunderstanding for future questions, was to draw a distinction. There was the SDS Deputies Club, the building, and of course there was the SDS Deputies Club consisting of the deputies as members; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: You mean people who gathered there? Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The people who were members of -- there was the club, which contained the members, being the SDS deputies.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, and also other people who were not deputies; they were not involved in politics, or in party politics in any way. It was just a place where people gathered. I think, if I'm not mistaken, that those might have been officially the premises of the party, but I'm not sure about that. Perhaps not officially. But meetings and consultations and seminars were held there on different topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, my apology. This may seem a bit cryptic or confused. It's only that at times over the weekend a lot of time got spent on sorting out a certain amount of question of whether one was talking about the building or the club and I was trying to stop that from happening here. I'll just go straight to it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever attend meetings of the SDS Deputies Club?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The Deputies Club as MPs, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, during your year of office, attend any SDS meetings at the SDS Deputies Club building?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were broader-based meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In what sense? What were they? Meetings of what group or body or what people?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I think that there was a political council and an economic council within the party. I think those were the names. That's where people from the party met, but first and foremost, experts on individual issues, and they would talk about such topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So were they separate meetings, the political council and economic council, or were they in practice wrapped into one?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes, they were separate meetings, but sometimes I think there were overlaps, so certain matters were discussed jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Roughly, what sort of attendance was there at meetings of that nature? How many people?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: About 20 to 30, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many of those meetings, as best you can remember, did you attend during the year that you were a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It's hard to say. Maybe about ten within a year, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Dr. Karadzic often or normally there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think that either individually or jointly, all leaders from the state authorities and the party attended. Sometimes they attended all together, sometimes individually, but they were there most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So was Mr. Koljevic there, at at least some of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik play an active part in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The same as all the others. It depended on the actual topic that was being discussed. And then, of course, the person most competent on any given topic would have a leading role, but no special role otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you remember on what topics Mr. Krajisnik ever took a leading role in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, during your year in the government, did you ever have any private meetings with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No -- well, actually, just once, when we met, when I was appointed minister. I was invited to meet Mr. Krajisnik, and that was the first time I met him, on that occasion, because we had not known each other before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You'd never met before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that meeting, when you were introduced to him, was that a -- was it a business or political meeting, or was it a more or less formal, short introduction? Could you give the Trial Chamber the feel of what was involved in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, it was a meeting of convenience, to meet and exchange a few words and maybe some initial experiences, and whether I could expect to be able to deal with issues having to do with economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik give you any specific instructions or directions as to any approach you should adopt at government meetings?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. Nothing worth mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he brief you or give you any directions as to SDS policy?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need. At that time, everybody knew about everybody's guidelines and policies, and so it would have been totally redundant to repeat any of that to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, apart from your position as -- in the two bodies that we specifically mentioned, the Disaster Relief Agency and the National Parole Board, were you from time to time during your membership with the Bosnia-Herzegovina government appointed to various ad hoc commissions or groups?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Apart from your position in the two bodies that we specifically mentioned, the Disaster Relief Agency and the National Parole Board, were you from time to time during your membership of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government appointed to various ad hoc commissions or groups?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions, in the period of time when certain inter-ethnic tensions were already rising and there were individual incidents in some places, and the government set up the so-called tripartite committees made up of representatives of three different ethnic groups in order to try to solve problems in the field and calm things down, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you give, please -- well, did you go to various places, including Bosanski Brod, Ilijas, and Bratunac, in the performance of that particular type of work?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to those three places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the work was in the nature of mediating disputes wherever they flared up, was it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If you failed successfully to mediate and calm down a situation, what would happen then?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: In theory, the more powerful players would be called upon for the next stage, in case there was a next stage. So more senior-level ministers or their assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you -- can you remember when you went to Bratunac on one of these missions?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't remember the date. February, March 1992? Something like that. But I really can't remember the date, or the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the specific problem which took you to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: There was a murder in the vicinity of Bratunac, some village in the area, and it led to ethnic tensions to such an extent that that murder was declared to have been caused by nationalist sentiment. And we went there and tried to place everything under the control of the state, the investigation and everything, and to stop people from taking justice into their own hands in any chaotic way. We wanted to make sure that everything was done in a proper and civilised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This was a murder of a member of one ethnic group by a member of another ethnic group, was it; and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: A Muslim had been killed, and the accused at the time -- afterwards, I don't know what happened, but the accused at the time was somebody who apparently was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this isn't a topic that I can cover in just five minutes, so that may be the right point for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do that after the break. But before we'll have a break, I've got one question in addition to what Mr. Stewart asked you. Mr. Antic, during the breaks of the parliamentary sessions, would the Serb or the SDS members of parliament, would they meet? I mean, if there was any problem where there was any need to further speak about it internally, would the members of parliament, of the SDS, meet? So the Deputies Club, that group of MPs, would they come together somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I believe that all Deputies Clubs had their premises, their offices, and they would all meet during breaks. That's as far as I know. I never participated in any of those meetings. I believe that this was customary at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, would they meet in the building you described as the Deputies Club or would they meet somewhere in the Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Assembly building, there were rooms which were their official premises for their meetings during breaks, and that was in the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope I didn't add to the confusion, but I now do understand that the Deputies Club that is a group of MPs would meet not in the building called the Deputies Club but in a room in the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Assembly building, they would meet during Assembly sessions, and that's where they would hold their club meetings. And during any other periods of time outside the Assembly session, they would meet in the club building. I hope I have not added to the confusion with what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's now perfectly clear. We'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any explanation why Defence is not in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no explanation has been communicated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait and time how much it takes us. Six interpreters, two technicians, one transcriber, three Prosecution. Could the Defence give any explanation why counsel is not there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Stewart is on his way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, my apologies. I asked Mr. Zahar to just explain to you very briefly why I'm late back in court. I was having a discussion with a representative of the Trial Chamber over a matter which did seem to be of some importance, and I apologise. I think we both, in the course of that discussion, probably -- it extended a little bit longer. But I hope Your Honours will accept my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from Mr. Zahar and you may proceed. But if you'd be fully dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. It's convenient sometimes for us to leave the material in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I hope Your Honours understand. I certainly wouldn't wish the discourtesy of simply ignoring the timetable or deliberately keeping Your Honours waiting, or even accidentally, inadvertently, keeping Your Honours waiting. I take it the examination of the witness hasn't proceeded without me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, although I was about to ask whether Mr. Krajisnik had any questions. I said at 11:05:53 that you could proceed, Mr. Stewart. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you arrived -- well, who went to Bratunac, then? Do you remember, Mr. Antic? There was you and then what colleagues of yours from the government went with you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: This was a very memorable journey for me. We went in a helicopter. There was Mr. Avdo Hebib, who was either the assistant minister for the interior or something to that effect. And there was somebody else there. I can't remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then when you got to Bratunac, what was your primary aim?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: To talk to both sides that were struck by panic. We spoke both to Muslim community and the Serbian community separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you then submit a report?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Of course. I didn't do it personally. Somebody on behalf of the commission submitted an official report to the president of the government and this was forwarded to higher instances. I don't know what happened next, because my role had ended with that site visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a report to the government, was it, or to whom?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Dr. Karadzic have any involvement in this particular work of, for example, going out to Bratunac in mediation capacity? I don't mean that he went to Bratunac himself, but your work of going to Bratunac, did Dr. Karadzic have any personal involvement in that particular work?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. I was delegated by the Prime Minister Jure Pelivan himself. Whether he had consulted somebody prior to that or not, I wouldn't know. I don't think so, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik have any part in this work?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there anything about that particular mission to Bratunac which caused you and your colleagues in the delegation any particular discomfort or concern?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, nothing directly. But the atmosphere was very tense, and in such an atmosphere, there is always a reason for concern. Something could always happen, an incident of some sort. That kind of concern existed, but generally speaking, there was no concern at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you had your meetings with the Serb leaders in the locality and the Muslim leaders in the locality, were they entirely peaceful, friendly meetings?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Peaceful, friendly, but still there was tension, there was electricity in the air; there was a lot of emotions, because the cause of our visit had nothing to do with things being peaceful. But there were no incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you able to make any observations about the extent to which arms were being held by the people in that locality?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed -- actually, I saw in the village where we were, in the Muslim part, I saw that people were armed, and they did not even go to great lengths to hide it from us. And I suppose that the Serbian side also had weapons, but they didn't demonstrate their weapons so openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did anybody attending any of the meetings that you held have any weapon with them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: At the meetings, inside, there were no visible signs of weapons; however, the people who were standing outside waiting for the outcome of those meetings, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did that apply to both Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Muslims now. I don't know about the Serbs. I did not see any, and I can't say whether they had weapons or not. I can only assume that they did, but I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you went to Bosanski Brod - perhaps I could lead on this to speed things up - were the tensions -- had the tensions in Bosanski Brod led to both sides, by which I mean the Serbs and the Muslims, setting up checkpoints dividing the town?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, on both sides. But actually, I believe that there were more Serbs and Croats than Serbs and Muslims. There was some participation of Muslims, but generally speaking, the division was between the Serbs and the Croats in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the Croat delegate in your mission take any specific steps to try to resolve the matter so far as Croats were concerned?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: We participated at the joint session of the municipality, where that leadership was. I don't know about their positions. The three of us - myself, the gentleman representing the Croat side and the gentleman representing the Muslim side - we tried to alleviate the tensions. We were of the opinion that the incidents had no real cause, and that's when we agreed that I should go and talk to the Serbian side, to the people who had put up barricades on that side, and the gentleman who was also a minister and whose name I can't remember at the moment - his first name was Miro - he went to the Croat side. I believe that he even went to Croatia proper to talk to people in Slavonski Brod about the ways to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say that you came to the opinion that the incidents had no real cause, did you form an opinion? You say "no real cause." What was the cause, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: At that time, there had been no shooting or killings or any of those things. It was just the reaction to a potential fear on both sides. In that sense, I don't think that there was any real cause. This was just in fear or in preparation of some possible future events. The situation was still under control. Everything was rather calm and peaceful at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did your delegation form any impression as to whether, whatever the causes were, they were essentially local or came from outside the municipality of Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: As I visited the people on the Serbian side, my impression was that the decision was not only at the local level, but even the micro-local level. In one part of the town. They did it spontaneously. It was a knee-jerk reaction. There was no plan. It was all a big improvisation. It just so happened, there was nothing premeditated about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did any member of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency visit Bosanski Brod as a follow-up to your mission?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Of course, after our visit we submitted a report to the Prime Minister. I believe that the Prime Minister forwarded that information to whoever, the president, the Presidency. And soon after that, Mrs. Plavsic, representing the Serbian side, Mr. Fikret Abdic, and I don't know who it was representing the Croat side, they went to the region soon after. And that's when my mission was completed. I only went for field visits, and I didn't have any other tasks as a follow-up to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, I don't want to ask you questions about a massacre said by some people, including a witness here, to have taken place at a certain place called Sijekovac, so I'm not asking about that. But you have heard of such an incident, have you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as you know, did that incident -- is that incident said to have taken place before or after your visit to Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this happened after. I'm sure that it happened after.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you also -- a group of the type that you've described, a delegation, went to Ilijas. Was that in or around March 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It is possible. I'm very bad at dates, I'm afraid. It is possible that it was in March. All the three visits happened within a very short time space.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able to say that it was in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Early 1992, if you consider March being early in the year. It was not winter, in any case. It was spring. The weather was rather good at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the issue there was this, was it: That the Serbs had detained a truck with ammunition and the local Muslims were complaining that the Serbs were proposing to retain those arms. Was that the issue?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did your delegation manage, one way or another, to put those arms under the control of the JNA in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: This is the only thing that we were successful with completely. We agreed that the truck was placed at our disposal and the army put that in a central depot. Both sides were happy with that. After that we had concrete talks with the Muslim side. Everybody was happy that this was arranged in that way. The person representing the army at that time was General Djurdjevac. I remember him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were the local Muslims satisfied with the solution that you achieved?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I believe so. They said so. They were afraid that the arms could be turned against them. And when the arms left the area, they were happy how this whole situation had been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were the -- was the central Muslim leadership, or the higher Muslim leadership of the SDA, happy with that solution, so far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can only assume that they were satisfied that the arms had been withdrawn from the area. I don't know whether they were satisfied that all these arms were put under the control of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Back to the government meetings. Did you, when you attended government meetings during your year in office, receive instructions in advance on how to vote?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, not in any organised manner. There was no need for that. 95 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. per cent of the issues pertaining to the work of the government did not have to be coordinated by anybody, because all these issues were professional issues and there was no need for instructions for any of these issues. As for the political issues, I personally was never instructed in any manner. I can't speak of my other colleagues in other ministries, whether they had any instructions from anybody. In any case, it was never done in an organised manner across the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you form any impression, from what you observed at those meetings, as to whether your HDZ or SDA colleagues were receiving instructions on how to vote?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I have already said that when we discussed the federal state and the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina in it, this was done. When it came to professional issues, one couldn't notice any influence. Professional issues are professional issues and they're not ethnically based.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the government, during your membership, address security issues?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can't say that this wasn't done formally, but there was nothing to it in essence. What it all boiled down to was the notorious political and security situation, and the formula was that this was very complex, that it had to be monitored in order to prevent any further escalation, escalations. This was just a formula provided to us by the SUP, without any details, save for some particular incidents that sometimes were discussed in somewhat greater detail. Otherwise, it was all just a formality. All these reports were just a formality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The foreign minister, the minister with responsibility for international relations, was a Muslim, Mr. Silajdzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did he at times during your year of office go on missions to other countries?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he report back to the government on his return from such visits?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: From time to time, with a lot of delay. Again, another formality, without any details. And sometimes he did not report at all. I found it strange that a government of any kind could have international relations that somebody could be sent on state visits without reporting back to the government. This was very strange to me, and I did not find that to be serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the -- his not reporting back to the government, was that in the face of any requests by you and your other government colleagues which were met by reluctance or refusal?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever made such requests. On some occasions, though, there were requests of the sort for him to report back on the visit. I believe that it was a visit to Turkey or some other Arabic country, and the response was: There is no need for me to report back to the government, because I went as a private individual, and the expenses were covered by my party, so this is not the matter for the government. In my view, this was very strange, because it was very strange for a minister in the government to visit a foreign state as a private individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you personally convinced by that explanation by Mr. Silajdzic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Of course not, but it was quite clear to me that there was no point in asking these questions because I was getting nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you recall when was the last meeting you attended as a member of the Bosnia and Herzegovina government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there was an official government meeting on that day, but my last presence within the government building and the cabinet, and on the occasion of the last session, I do remember that date, because it's quite poignant. It was on the 3rd of April, 1992, and it was a joint meeting, or an extended meeting, or whatever you want to call it, of the entire leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina; all the government ministers, the BH Presidency, the president of the Assembly, the army representatives, and some others, Territorial Defence, I believe, and some other people from the overall political life within the country. So that happened on the 3rd of April. And it was convened due to some problems in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm whether the -- if the following people were present: Mr. Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stjepan Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nikola Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mrs. Plavsic there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not sure. She should have been there. Everybody who was supposed to be there was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Karadzic there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. He wasn't there, because it was just for the official authorities, people who had posts within the executive branch of the government, and he didn't have such a post at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In what capacity, as far as you could see, was Mr. Krajisnik there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: He attended in the same way as everybody else; the president of the Assembly, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you regard the president of the Assembly as part of the executive branch of the government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was anybody else present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness complete his answer. You said: "No, but ..." so you may have had something in mind. Could you explain to us what you had in mind when you said: "No, but ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
