utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I was about to say is I don't know whether he was just present to hear about these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it's fair, Your Honour, if I make it clear that of course I don't have the slightest objection or concern about Your Honour's question. I believe I didn't attempt to cut off the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't blame you for that. But since you started your next question and since I was interested to know what came after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't take any criticism, Your Honour. The transcript might make it look as if I had. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the events in Bijeljina were the instigator of that meeting. What was reported or understood at that meeting to have been happening in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to specify anything without speculating. I don't know about the details. I know there were some incidents, there were requests on the part of Alija Izetbegovic for the army to get involved in sorting the situation out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were there any differences of view at that meeting between Mr. Izetbegovic and any of the Serbs who were present?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: There was general disagreement about this. Do we want to use the army to sort things out or not? If we do use the Armed Forces, we have to use them everywhere. Whereas Mr. Izetbegovic insisted on the Armed Forces being brought in in Bijeljina only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, did he have a point of view which he expressed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did General Kukanjac have a point of view which he expressed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The general was willing to make the army available in order to help solving all the burning issues in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but of course, if there was agreement on all sides, in the same way everywhere. And of course there had to be agreement on every occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did it appear why Mr. Izetbegovic was insisting on the JNA being brought in to Bijeljina only?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I gleaned it on the basis of the overall context. That is to say, apparently there were some Serb groups in Bijeljina causing trouble, and that was a kind of invitation for the army to act against these Serb groups. That was my understanding as to why Bijeljina. It must have been something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was -- in the end, was the JNA used to attempt to quell disorders in different locations around Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you take steps the very next morning to move your family to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the next morning I took my family to Belgrade, not because wanted to move away from Sarajevo but because there was a case [Realtime transcript read in error "indication"] of death in my family. My sister-in-law had died, and so I took my wife and my children to Belgrade in order for my wife to be able to help look after her young children. So it was a temporary family emergency, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You personally had difficulties returning, did you, because disorder broke out in Sarajevo and there was a suspension of air travel?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I drove my family to Belgrade, and my intention was to leave them there and go back to Sarajevo on Sunday, on the 5th. But, as you said, there was no flight, and I remember quite correctly that Mr. Ejub Ganic was trying to catch the same flight from Belgrade to Sarajevo and we were grounded. So I stayed on for a couple more days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is this right: You returned after a few days to Sarajevo, that you went to your parents in Rajkovica and you stayed there until sometime in May 1992? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart. There's one answer I did not fully understand. You said, Witness, that there was an indication of death in your family because your sister-in-law had died. I had some difficulties understanding what indication he exactly means. Did your sister-in-law die early April, 1st, 2nd, or 3rd of April, so immediately previous to your driving to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. A couple of months earlier she was killed in a car accident in Serbia. Nothing to do with war or anything. But we in the family all took turns in taking care of her children. Sometimes my mother or my wife or somebody else, because they were very young.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You moved to Pale sometime in May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What instigated your move to Pale?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I was appointed minister of the economy at the Assembly of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it used to be called then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- do you remember when in May you first arrived in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember correctly, but if I was elected on the occasion of this Assembly, I know, I remember that it was on the 12th of May, so at some point after that. Three, four, five, seven days later; I can't remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you arrived in Pale, you first lived in the Kikinda building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you in fact given the task of -- essentially of forming the ministry in the government of the Serb Republic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct, from the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you receive detailed instructions as to how to go about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: There was nobody to give any detailed instructions. There was nothing. The conditions were not good. And so we based ourselves on our own experiences and know-how and our ideas as to what should be done first, and then we worked on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long overall did you remain in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: You mean as a member of government in the government building in Pale? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes. You may answer that question. Yes, how long did you remain in Pale as a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The government, as a body, at Pale -- well, I think that we moved to Jahorina in the beginning of June because the conditions were not very good at the Kikinda building, and there wasn't enough space, simply, and so we moved to Bistrica Hotel at Jahorina. And I remained within the government until the end of the year, at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How would you describe, very briefly, how would you describe the nature of your particular tasks and responsibilities as that minister?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Quite briefly, it was necessary to set up some regulatory framework for the functioning of the economy in the conditions which were characterised by an imminent threat of war and a rather disturbed economy, cut off communications. We had to put a stop and prevent the looting, any behaviour which would be out of control, any anarchy, and regulate things as much as possible and bring about some kind of normal order, in order to avoid chaos, quite briefly. And all that with the aim of ensuring a level of the functioning of the economy, in order to ensure the survival of the population, in order to avoid any further wasting of resources. And we were all expecting things to calm down relatively quickly at that stage, and of course we wanted to prevent the economy from going under. And in order to make it possible to revive the economy as soon as possible after the troubles ended, and we all hoped that it would happen sooner rather than later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any one person to whom you particularly reported?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Of course. The president of the government, the head of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... have been your professor at university?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, from when you arrived in Pale in May 1992, over the next few months, did you have meetings yourself with Mr. Krajisnik? And I should say, I'm not talking about large meetings at which you and he might have both been present. You understand what I mean: Did you actually have meetings with Mr. Krajisnik himself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not very often. Very rarely, in fact. But mostly about individual issues having to do with the economy, and first and foremost, because he had a great deal of experience in this field. So it was about getting advice as to how to solve certain issues, because he was familiar with the larger structures and systems within the region, so that was the basis for our meeting, not in his capacity as the president of the Assembly but as an experienced businessman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say to the Trial Chamber with what frequency such meetings took place between you and Mr. Krajisnik? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, not very often. Perhaps five to six times during my time in office, perhaps not even that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware of or did you see any evidence of Mr. Krajisnik's participation in the executive aspects of government in the Serb Republic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik never participated in the work of the government, and generally speaking, an unwritten rule was for every branch to mind their own business, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware of, after your arrival in Pale in May 1992, were you aware of any organ or body with the title "Expanded Presidency"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: When I got to Pale, I was elected to some assembly as a member of government, and it was on the same occasion when the Presidency of the Republic, of the Serb Republic, was elected. And obviously, I do know that there was a Presidency, and I had also heard of the expression "Extended Presidency," which implied advisory meetings of the Presidency with other branches of government, other advisory bodies in those instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'd like to put a question, one or two questions, to the witness to clarify his meetings with Mr. Krajisnik, as you said, as an experienced businessman. Could you give us an example of the issues you discussed with him. You said: "So it was about getting advice as to how to solve certain issues." Could you give us an example of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't actually remember any specific incidents at the moment, but since in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in particular, there were many large companies, and they all had their headquarters in Sarajevo and they all had branch offices or subsidiaries in other parts of the country. And following the breakup of the Republic, those systems, those large companies, were dissolved. And so it was a problem as to how to bring them back together, such as Energoinvest or another company for oil and oil derivatives, et cetera. So it was about these large companies, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned oil and oil derivatives. Was that one of your concerns, where to get oil? Because everyone, I would say including a government, would need oil. Was that an issue you would discuss with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, not in terms of supplies, but in terms of organising or structuring the parts of companies, and the company in question was Energopetrol and they were in charge of oil distribution. And obviously, I had cooperation with these companies. I was trying to help them function, and up until such point in time when they could take care of everything independently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you then did in organising and structuring the Energopetrol to make it properly function again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing special, really. There was this breakdown and I found appropriate people to lead the company, who enjoyed the trust of the employees as well, and they were people of integrity, people with a certain amount of experience, and they continued to work as if everything were normal. So that was the end of my task. I couldn't tell them what to do exactly in their day-to-day work, but I could help them get started. Because the government, of course, had to take account of these big companies and try to do something about them. And as for the SMEs, they had to fend for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you were not responsible and you were not involved in where to -- how to get oil, who was responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ministry was responsible, but in the last analysis, it was up to the companies that were entrusted with that task by the ministry. It was up to them in as far as the civilian uses were concerned. I'm not talking about the military or anything like that. That was not within my area of competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for civilian purposes, you were responsible in getting the oil from somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ministry is not involved in the purchase of oil or getting supplies or anything; it was up to the companies to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the companies also do sell it to the government, do they not? I mean, the government needs fuel as well, or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, for civilian purposes, you were responsible for -- you say the companies were responsible. Of course, there are two parties, isn't it; the one who buys and the one who sells.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The company buys and sells. They're involved in trade. Energopetrol bought oil and oil derivatives and then sold them on to any other companies that might be needing them, at market prices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then did you directly, for government purposes, for civilian government purposes, buy oil from Energopetrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From whom did you buy it, if not from Energopetrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean -- who do you mean when you say "you"? Do you mean the government or the ministry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your ministry, being a part of the government, isn't it? But tell us first about the ministry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I got it. Right. Our ministry needed fuel for cars, and that was all. Is that what you mean? We didn't have any huge needs. There were a number of petrol stations owned by Energopetrol and that's where we bought our petrol and they invoiced it to us and then we paid it. Actually, the finance ministry paid for all this expenditure for all the other ministries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. You say the fuel needed for cars was directly purchased from Energopetrol at the gas stations and was paid directly. And now, apart from the ministry, the government; you made a distinction. How about the government, their supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there was never -- did the government never buy quantities of fuel, apart from getting it at the gas stations, from Energopetrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When we talk in terms of the technical needs, for the day-to-day functioning of the government, cars, vehicles, in general, yes, that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to my knowledge. Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as far as the military is concerned, that was done by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not involved in that, and the military had their own special channels through the Defence Ministry or whatever, but I was never involved in any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as far as petrol is concerned, your meetings with Mr. Krajisnik were limited to finding people to be appointed? I'm just trying to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned the nature of these talks, and now you've mentioned fuel. But we talked about other companies, such as Sipad, which is a furniture manufacturers, and the woods and timber resources in the Republika Srpska, and all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, but I put these questions to you since you mentioned oil companies and I was interested to know a bit more about that. So but your meetings as far as oil company, or an oil company was concerned, was limited to finding the right people to be appointed in the parts that remained in your part of the former Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I didn't consult him about the right people or anything like that. I just sought advice on a number of issues, different things that we might have discussed, and I managed to find the people myself, or else they came to me and they were perhaps suggested by somebody else from the company itself. It wasn't a kind of choice of people in normal terms, because people scattered and many of them fled, so it was a bit of a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you just sought advice on a number of issues, not specifically finding the right people. What kind of issues did you seek his advice on, specifically in relation to oil companies or Energopetrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never about that. I just gave you an example of all the activities that I had to go through in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you tell us that -- I mean, you came with -- you told us about companies for oil and oil derivatives. I asked you about it. You came with the example of Energopetrol. I asked you what you discussed, and you said something about restructuring and finding -- you were trying to help them function and that -- well, you gave that as an example. And now I ask you a bit further about it, whether it was about staffing and the management. You say, No, it wasn't. And I asked you, What else, then, was it that you discussed, what other issues? As you said, you were seeking the advice of Mr. Krajisnik. And you said nothing specific. It's difficult for me to get the right impression to what extent your discussions of companies with oil and oil derivatives, what they -- what the subject specifically was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously you misunderstood me. I mentioned some of the things that had to do with my activities, and then you mentioned oil. I was in charge of all of that. I didn't want to say that we discussed specifically this or that or the other. Every now and then when I had an issue to raise, I would raise it. I can't remember exactly what issues I raised. My meetings were -- with Krajisnik were of that nature. They were not political meetings. And this is what I wanted to say. I did not want to specify any of the issues. I remember that I worked on my own. I was very independent in my work, if that is what you were referring to. I never had to seek Mr. Krajisnik's approval on any of the issues that I had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about approval, but you came up with companies for oil and oil derivatives. You are the one who mentioned Energopetrol as the firm involved. You said: "And the company in question was Energopetrol, and they were in charge of distribution." So you came with the examples, and I asked you what specifically you discussed in relation to this firm with Mr. Krajisnik. And I have not received an answer yet, apart from that -- nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nothing, nothing. I told you what I did with the company Energopetrol and what its role was. This is what I told you. I found people; I remember that. This was just by chance that I came across people who could be appointed directors at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to understand why you went to Mr. Krajisnik on five or six occasions, and you say that you considered him an experienced businessman. Why did you consider him an experienced businessman? What did you base that knowledge on? What did you base that information on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a well-known fact. Mr. Krajisnik was one of the leading directors in one of the biggest companies in Sarajevo, Energoinvest, which was the market leader in the region, and he was well aware of the issues, and everybody knew that, everybody was aware of that. He had experience in the job. I talked to a number of other people who could help me with ideas, with things. I would talk to other people as well, because I had to start from scratch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you said that you had considered him an experienced businessman, and you say that you considered him that because he had been one of the directors in this energy-producing company. But why did you consider him as an experienced businessman? Was he well known in the community as somebody who had a role in the local economy, who had dealt with various parts of the economy? Was he famous for that? Was he an experienced politician, a member of the Assembly? Why did you have to contact him for advice in your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was generally known as a good businessman, and it was not only in my case, but everybody knew him as such. Why I contacted him, of all the people, on several occasions is hard to say, but I contacted dozens of others; in the country, outside of the country, in the government. I would contact anybody whom I thought could give me advice and answers to my questions. It was a normal thing for me, and I really don't know how else I could explain that, what other explanation to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you know about his business experience that could portray him as an expert? What things did you know of him that would indicate to you that he was an economic expert? You told us a while ago that you didn't know much about him, that he hadn't met him before. What made you think that he was somebody who was well abreast of the economy, that he was an economic professional? What did you know from his CV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know him personally, as I'm a bit younger than him. However, his company had been a very hot issue in Sarajevo for a number of years, and the workers were happy, they had good salaries, they all had apartments. Nobody who knew anything about the economy was -- who didn't know about Mr. Krajisnik. The Prime Minister was a teacher, Mr. Karadzic was a doctor, Mrs. Plavsic was a biologist. And it was only logical if there was somebody for me to talk to, it would have been somebody who had been a businessman before. And among the people that I've just mentioned, Mr. Krajisnik was the most experienced one in that respect, and everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your view, for how long was he a director of that company, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. More than ten years, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your answers, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, the Extended Presidency, or Expanded Presidency, that's all the same thing, is it, in your mind?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The Extended Presidency is the same thing as what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think the question is implicitly answered, Your Honour. I was only concerned, Your Honour, we get these translations -- I get "Extended --" no criticism. "Extended Presidency" comes back sometimes in English as the translation and I just want to be clear that there's no difference between "extended" and "expanded," that it's just a minor interpretation question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not the Presidency, but I would say a widened Presidency, whether it's expanded or extended, that doesn't make any difference for you? I don't know whether this is difficult to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's hard, Your Honour, because we put that question and then it comes in Serbian to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, I'm asking you questions, really, about the Presidency and then something that I put to you as being Expanded Presidency. There wasn't any other sort of larger Presidency in the Republika Srpska apart from something that you had heard of described as "the Expanded Presidency," was there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There was a Presidency. I have heard of the term "Expanded" or "Extended Presidency," which is all the same. You're asking me if there was a body even wider than that. Could you please be more precise? I'm not very clear on what you want from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In passing, your last answer has come to the point -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know whether -- You say there was the Presidency and there was something which was called the Expanded or Extended Presidency. Could you tell us what the difference is between Presidency Sec and Extended or Expanded Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presidency, as such, was an official body elected by the Assembly, composed of three members; namely, Karadzic, Koljevic, and Plavsic. And the Extended or Expanded Presidency is a term that became known as the extended sessions of the Presidency whenever consultations were needed. This is how I perceive that. This is the Extended Presidency that sometimes would involve some other people, as far as I know. I did not participate in any of those sessions, so I wouldn't really be able to tell you exactly what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what you heard, who would then attend these extended meetings of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to the Presidency proper, consisting of three members, those sessions were often or mostly attended by the president of the Assembly, the Prime Minister, and sometimes some ministers; the minister of the police, the minister of the army. It largely depended on the situation at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. May I make it clear when I was suggesting that his last answer at line 22 had covered the point, I simply meant the point about the terminology "expanded" or "extended" rather than the larger question. But thank you. Your Honour's questions have gone into that helpfully, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever attend yourself any meeting which you regarded as a meeting of that Expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you regard Mr. Djeric as a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you regard the Expanded Presidency as something which had clear membership, so that you could say, well, A, B, C, D, E, F, whatever, are members and X, Y, Z are not members? Is that the way you saw that particular entity?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: You're referring to a specific composition. No, I did not regard it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you able, when you were in Pale, to gain any clear idea from your own observations and knowledge as to who controlled military matters?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The military matters were controlled by the Presidency of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you say "the Presidency of the Republic," which individuals did that mean, in your assessment, controlled the army? Or controlled military -- well, the army, military matters.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency, Karadzic, and the members of the Presidency, Plavsic and Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you able yourself to form any impression of the relative involvement and influence of those three people on the army?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I did not have an occasion to measure that, but I believe that, according to the hierarchy, the president had the biggest influence. It was a collective body, and I really don't know how they shared the level of influence amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you, in 1992, from May onwards, when you were in Pale, did you observe or come to know of anything which indicated to you that Mr. Krajisnik had any control over army or police activities?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. There were no indications of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, at government meetings, discuss from time to time the question of prison camps?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a number of so-called collection centres, prisons, or whatever they were called at the time, and on several occasions we received information about them. And it was the government's position that they should be placed under control of the regular bodies, that there should be order, that there should be investigations, and finally a decision was made that all of those should be closed down. In a nutshell, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the issue of prison camps or detention centres -- well, what was your own -- apart from attending meetings of the government, what was your own personal involvement in any questions relating to prison camps or detention centres?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever. My only involvement was my presence at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there particular individual members of the government who did have specific responsibilities or duties in relation to that matter?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I believe that those were minister of the defence, minister of the police, and minister of justice. This was within their purview, and as a government, we just adopted positions on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- were you present when reports were received by the government that caused you special concern or anxiety as to the position? I'm talking about prison camps and detention centres, just to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Whether I was present?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Whether you were -- you remember being present -- I'll put the question again, Mr. Antic, so it's clear. Whether you remember being present at any meetings of the government at which reports were received in relation to prison camps or detention centres which caused you personally particular anxiety or concern.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I was present, yes. A commission had inspected those camps and submitted a report about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that caused you concern, did it, that report?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, not really. As far as I remember, there were stories that the government had not even been aware of. Some of those stories were true, some were not true. The task of the commission was to investigate into all of those stories and submit a report. I don't remember all of the details, but the commission said that there were some irregularities but also there was false information. They suggested some things that should be implemented by the Ministry of Justice, the police, and the army, and it was the government's position that this issue had to be placed under the control of the army and that such centres, or whatever you want to call them, or whatever they were called at the time, should be closed down as soon as possible. And I believe that soon after that they indeed were closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Mr. Krajisnik -- or do you know of Mr. Krajisnik being involved in any discussions or decisions in relation to prison camps or detention centres?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik have any particular reputation, personal reputation, so far as his dealings with the Muslim community was concerned?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Any particular reputation? I don't know. My view is, and it was also a prevalent view at the time, that Mr. Krajisnik was a patient man, that he is a good negotiator, and that he was familiar with the mentality of these people with whom he had spent his whole, entire life. He had the reputation of a person who could talk reasonably with the Muslims about certain issues that were at stake throughout all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware of how the Muslim political leadership regarded Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't know this as a fact, but my impression is, if somebody wanted to talk to him -- actually, if they wanted to talk to anybody, it would be him rather than anybody else from the leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or read or see, on television or in person, any statements by Mr. Krajisnik which were abusive or aggressive or disparaging of Muslims or the Muslim nation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it right that towards the end of 1992 you left your post as a member of the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It is true that I left the position, but not voluntarily. The president of the government resigned, and by law, the entire government had to resign. That's how I left my position. And later on I was never elected as a member of the subsequent government. I got involved with something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the something else, you took up a task, didn't you, of formation of a Chamber of Commerce of Republika Srpska and, apart from your own personal commercial activities, that's where you channelled your energies from then onwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock, and at the same time, the back of my mind, the 65 ter summary. I wonder whether -- how much time you'd still need so as to see whether we should continue after the break. About -- I'm not quite sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's two things, Your Honour. I can say, first of all, I'm very near the end; but secondly, it would, if that were acceptable to Your Honour, be slightly more convenient just to wrap up the last few questions after a break rather than before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you then still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I guess not more than about ten minutes or so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break now until 10 minutes to 1.00, and if we all arrive in time, you might be able to finish at about 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say straight away that I -- my estimate of ten minutes, which still stands, was the questions I had in mind, but Mr. Krajisnik has transmitted a number of points to me, so I would probably require a little longer. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, may I show you, please, a document which has previously been in evidence, exhibited more than once, in fact, but P43 is the most convenient number. Now, it should be a document of several pages in your own language, Mr. Antic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Antic, I know you have seen this document since you arrived in The Hague. Let there be no mystery or surprise about how that's happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have a copy of that document before us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. -- it is a document of the 19th of December, and if the questioning goes in the direction I anticipate, then we might not to have a close look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We only wished to know which document it was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. Sorry. I certainly hadn't intended to cause any hitches for the Prosecution. It's the one numbered 93. It's that version, which has generally been taken as the one that we will use normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although now you're confusing me, because P43 is number 100. But I do not mind. It's the 19th of December, and if we put it on the ELMO, the copy which is presented to the witness, then we know exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the numbering confusion, Your Honour. That comes from having a document which says on it P43 and P64A, and so on. But it's unlikely to make a material difference this morning -- this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, my question is, therefore, had you ever seen this document or some very similar document in essentially the same form before you came to The Hague over the last few days?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, if I tell you it's a document which has come to be very widely known as Variants A and B, had you -- before you came here to The Hague, had you heard of a document described or labelled as "Variants A and B"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you present at any large meeting of the SDS in the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo in late 1991 or early 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you -- changing -- thank you. That's the end of that -- my questions on that topic, Mr. Antic. Can you remember what the public position of Mr. Krajisnik was during the war on the question of whether Serbs should leave or remain in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: You mean after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, at any time, before or after Dayton.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik was always fighting for the survival of Serbs in Sarajevo, as he was born in Sarajevo, and me too, and I think he always strove to ensure that Serbs could continue to live in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you ever recall him taking a public position that Serbs should leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, would it become clearer if, especially since we're talking about a long range in time, perhaps to make -- Sarajevo was a city which at times was divided and -- to make any distinction in your questioning on this? I mean, parts of what now -- what used to be Sarajevo, because Pale was one of the municipalities, I -- "staying in Sarajevo" is an ambiguous expression if the context is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm thinking about it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could specifically ask the witness, If you say that Mr. Krajisnik was fighting for the survival of Serbs in Sarajevo, if we split that up, would he have been in favour of Serbs remaining in Serb Sarajevo before Dayton or would he also express himself on Serbs remaining on, well, to say Muslim-controlled parts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, staying in Sarajevo, and that solution for Sarajevo had to be found through negotiations, how the government had to work. It was still very much an open question, and nobody claimed to know what the final solution was going to be. So it would all depend on a solution for Sarajevo. But generally speaking, to be able to remain in Sarajevo, whatever the solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But when there was no solution yet, would he promote Serbs remaining in non-Serb-controlled areas of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In case there was no solution of what kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you were talking about a solution, I take it. During -- before Dayton, we know that there was a part of Sarajevo under Serb control and a part of Sarajevo under Muslim or -- well, let's say Muslim control. Did Mr. Krajisnik ever express his views on whether Serbs should remain in those parts of Sarajevo that were under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never heard of any public statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, after Dayton, after Dayton, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After Dayton --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still had a split, although the lines were a bit different, perhaps, but we still had parts of what used to be greater Sarajevo, that means including Pale, under Serb control, and other parts under Muslim control. Did he, after Dayton, say that those who -- those Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbs that were living in Muslim-controlled part of Sarajevo, that they should stay or not stay or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what the general attitude of the leadership and Mr. Krajisnik was, that they should stay where they were. And as to who was going to do what later, well, quite a few municipalities, such as Ilidza, for example, were given to Muslims, according to Dayton, and at least 50 per cent were Serbs. So it would be logical for them to stay where they were. So that was what Mr. Krajisnik advocated, as well as all of us who could be expected to give some kind of opinion. That was the logical conclusion, but unfortunately, people acted differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, during the time that you were in Pale in 1992, were you aware of there being any detention facilities in the municipality of Pale? No doubt there were some ordinary prisons that had always been there, but were you aware of any substantial detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with anything of the sort. I don't think it ever existed there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Specifically, were you aware of any location in Pale where Muslims were held in significant numbers during 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there in fact any prison at all of any sort in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't think there was any prison at all. At least, I don't know of any prison, any official prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the entity known as Novi Privrednik?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Novi Privrednik was basically an idea to organise a shareholding company so that many people would make small investments and for that company thus created to start providing opportunities for economic cooperation in a broader sense. So it was a shareholders' company, and the idea was for it to be set up and grow. But as far as I can remember, it never did make any headway. It was a simple shareholders' company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it somebody's brainchild?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who the father was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When was this idea first -- well, when did this idea first spring up?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Perhaps by the end of 1991, roughly speaking. Maybe later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have any involvement?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I knew of it, but I don't really think much was done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure I asked you this: Did Mr. Krajisnik ever attend any meeting of the government at which you were present in Pale, the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't think so, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Antic, you'll now be cross-examined by, I take it, Mr. Margetts, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Margetts, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic -- sorry. Microphone is now on. Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Antic, you referred to a meeting that you attended of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 3rd of April, 1992, and various comments that Alija Izetbegovic made at that meeting. We're in receipt of a tape-recording of the session of the Presidency which was held on the same day. Did you attend the session of the Presidency as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At the session of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic described the problem in Bijeljina as follows. He said: "In Bijeljina, a paramilitary unit entered the town, Arkan's unit. People were killed and wounded and the killings are still going on." Are they the same words he used to describe the situation in Bijeljina in the government session?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether it was in the same way, exactly the same words, but along these lines, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But you understood the problem in Bijeljina was the killing of civilians by Arkan's units?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: As to this information, the fact that it was a problem that they raised at that meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Secondly, Mr. Izetbegovic proposed, when speaking to Kukanjac, that the reserve TO forces should be mobilised, and he described the crisis points as follows: He said: "The crisis points that I've mentioned are Bijeljina, Kupres, Mostar, Banja Luka, and Bosanski Brod." Did he describe all of those places as places that required some security to be provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't receive the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could you answer that question again, please. Are those the places that Mr. Izetbegovic described as places where security was required?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he asked for intervention in Bijeljina only, and those were crisis situations, the ones that you mentioned. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But do you understand that it's quite possible that in the Presidency session he had in fact requested that security be provided for places other than Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Perhaps at the Presidency meeting. I'm not aware of that. But at the meeting where I was, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a binder of documents that I'd like to provide to the Court and the parties, and also a copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first document that I'd like to refer to is the document that's contained behind the tab 1A, and if Mr. Antic could be shown that document. And Your Honour, if I could have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P979, Your Honours, and the English translation, P979.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, do you have before you a document headed "Guidelines on tasks, modes of action --"

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Antic. Do you have before you this document that is headed "Guidelines on tasks, modes of action and functioning of defence forces of state organs and subjects, in the field of economy and social activities in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the state of war"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, this document was presented to the government on the 14th of July, 1992, at a session where you were present. Do you recall seeing this document at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember this document at all. This is the first I've ever seen of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, to possibly assist you, I'd like to refer you to the next document, which is at tab 1B, and that's a document titled "Operative programme of measures to prevent social disruption in conditions of a state of war," and is the previous exhibit number P583, tab 76. Mr. Antic, this second document, P583, is a document that was discussed at three different government sessions that you attended, namely, the session on the 16th of July, 1992; the session on the 22nd of July, 1992; and a further session I don't have before me. Nevertheless, seeing that document, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, just for my -- you say a document dated the 17th was discussed on the 16th. I'm just trying to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document that you have before you is one of the drafts of this document, and it was anticipated on the 16th of July and delivered on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, could I refer you to the first paragraph of this document, and you'll see that the first paragraph reads as follows: "Pursuant to Article 8 of the Law on Defence and with reference to the Guidelines on the tasks and the methods of action and functioning of defence forces, state authorities, and entities in the economy and public services of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in conditions of a state of war, the Government hereby adopts this operative programme of measures to prevent social disruption in conditions of a state of war." Does that assist you in reviewing the first document I showed you? I now ask you to refer back to that, document 1A in your binder. And does that assist you? You do remember this operative programme of measures. And do you remember the fact that that operative programme of measures was a programme intended to implement the guidelines at tab 1A of the binder?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember these guidelines. Of course, I do remember the programme. Apparently it says in the preamble that on the basis of the guidelines, they were entrusted with the task of preparing the programme for the government. All that is fine. That was something that I was myself involved in. But the first bit, I really don't know these guidelines. I can't recall any of that. I've never set eyes on this. Perhaps the president of the government had that, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In light of your knowledge as to how documents were prepared, the fact that there's such a specific reference to the guidelines in this first paragraph of the operative measures, can you say, looking at it today, that it's clear that the operative programme was intended to implement these guidelines?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I really don't know what it says in the guidelines. If that's what it says, probably, yes. Whether it's in its entirety or in terms of some details, I can't comment on it because I haven't read the text. If it says what you say it says, then apparently it is in line with the guidelines. I can't tell you because I haven't read the guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, I can refer you to section 6 of the guidelines. That's the first document. And that's a section headed "Tasks in the field of economy," and the first three -- the first paragraph under that heading is paragraph 18. It's on page 7 of your copy, in tab 1A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that the witness is looking at the operative measures. If the witness could be referred back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you're referring to chapters, because I take sections to be the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm referring to the chapters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Chapter 6. You'll find it on page 7 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, there's a description of the tasks associated with the field of economy, set out at paragraphs 18, 19, and 20. Could you read those paragraphs and confirm that they were the tasks that were part of your portfolio as minister for the economy.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. We'll come back to some of those tasks later on, but for the moment I'd now like to move to another topic, and that's the topic of the Extended or Expanded Presidency, as it was referred to in your evidence. Mr. Antic, as a minister, you received the Official Gazette of the Republic of Srpska, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, the government and the ministry received the Official Gazette. Of course we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And it was your habit to read it; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read it, and if there was nothing interesting from my point of view, for my particular sector, then I would not dwell on it for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: A decision that was published in the Official Gazette number 7 was a decision on amending the constitution, that stated as follows, that: "During a state of war, the Presidency is expanded with the following members: The president of the National Assembly and the Prime Minister of the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Did you read that decision on or around June 1992, when that decision was passed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact that this existed and that this was in place for war conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And as far as you understand it, a War Presidency did in fact function that included the three members - Karadzic, Koljevic, and Plavsic - and also included Krajisnik and Djeric; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Karadzic, Koljevic, and Plavsic were the members of the Presidency. I am not sure that the War Presidency, as such, existed. I actually don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, you attended the November 1992 session of the Assembly of the Serbian People that was held in Zvornik. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It is possible. Can you please jog my memory a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. One of the major issues on the agenda at this Assembly was an issue raised by Milan Trbojevic, the deputy Prime Minister, and that was the fact that the War Presidency was in fact functioning, despite the failure to fulfil the technical precondition for its function, namely, the formal declaration of a state of war. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, to jog your memory further: In the course of that discussion at the Assembly at which you were present, Karadzic said that he was all in favour of the Presidency because there's a lot of work to be done, and if Mr. Koljevic and he are busy, he can have Biljana, and if she is busy, then we have Mr. Krajisnik. He said that, We'd never come into conflict in the Presidency, and he said that they put all their ideas on the table and effectively they decide things collectively. Do you recall those comments being made by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember those words and I don't even remember that I was present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, we're spending a lot of time again on an issue that has been raised several, several times. This witness testified that mostly these sessions of the -- he said in addition to the Presidency proper, consisting of three members, those sessions - and he was talking about either extended meetings of the Presidency or meetings of the Expanded Presidency - he says: "Most of these -- most often or mostly attended by the president of the Assembly ..." I mean, do we have to go for ages again over -- the Chamber of course is aware of the disagreement on whether it existed or not, but there seems to be not major disagreement about presence and what was said about it and also on -- I think there are quite some documents on presence as well. So I wonder whether we have to go through it, again, until you come up with something new. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Unfortunately, I had nothing new in mind, and I thank you very much for your guidance on that. I'll proceed to the next topic, which still involves the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, 1992, at the 15th Session of the Presidency, that was attended by, among others, Mr. Krajisnik, the various tasks for the members of the Presidency were divided, and Mr. Krajisnik was delegated with the task of commissioners, and also with the task as the responsible person for the economy. Mr. Antic, you referred in your evidence to meetings that you had with Mr. Krajisnik where you discussed the economy. You said that that was because he was an eminent businessman. But in fact, the reason was that he was the representative in the Presidency responsible for that portfolio. That's the reason you met with him, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. I have never heard that this was his duty. I just knew him, and that's why I consulted him. I never knew that he was in charge of the economic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, also you said that it was the Presidency that commanded the military. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you said that you never attended any meetings of this War Presidency. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 27th of June, 1992, there was a meeting of the Presidency where Radovan Karadzic was not present, and an order was issued by Mr. Krajisnik, Koljevic, Plavsic, and Djeric, to the military, to cease artillery action in the area of Dobrinja. It is the case, isn't it, Mr. Antic, that it was not only Mr. Karadzic that had the power to order the military.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Koljevic and Plavsic as well probably. I really don't know what the division was among the three of them and what were their authorities, whether he himself, on his own, was in charge of issuing orders or whether that power was shared with Koljevic and Plavsic. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But you're not in a position to dispute the document that I have before me, are you? You're not in a position to dispute the fact that these four people ordered the military, because you weren't at these sessions, were you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they issued orders or not. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, you talked about some restricted functions you had as minister of the economy, and we've seen the description of those functions in the document that was Exhibit 1A, the guidelines. And that included responsibility for ensuring production of goods necessary for the war effort, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we're talking about the requirements at the time, we're talking about food articles, and any other goods, because any war activity requires a lot of different types of goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, if I could refer you back to the document that's at tab 1B of your materials, and that is the document that's Exhibit P583, tab 76, "The operative programme of measures to prevent social disruption." And in particular, if I could refer to you paragraphs 12 and 13 of that document. Do you have those paragraphs before you, Mr. Antic? Paragraph 12 states that: "There will be a wartime production plan for enterprises in the defence industry and both the Defence Ministry and the Ministry of the Economy are responsible for that." That's a correct description of your role in the production of military equipment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: This is a correct description of the Ministry of Defence. However, many companies were combined civilian and military, and that's why both the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Defence were jointly in charge, because the companies were of a dual nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Paragraph 13 states -- refers to the requirements in terms of supplying materiel and equipment and other sources, including weapons, ammunition, and equipment, and that responsibility falls to the Defence Ministry. Is it correct that that responsibility also fell within your area of jurisdiction, that is, that was a responsibility of the Ministry of the Economy as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It was by and large the Ministry of Defence. Some of it may have concerned the Ministry of Economy, but as far as the materiel and the technical equipment was concerned, it was primarily the Ministry of Defence that was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You say some of it may have concerned the Ministry of the Economy. Are you saying that as Minister of the Economy it fell within your jurisdiction to distribute weapons? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, although that was outside your jurisdiction, did you in fact order or request that weapons be distributed to specific commanders?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: Commanders? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you request that weapons be issued to commanders of crisis staffs?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in The Hague, I saw that document. It is a letter - if we're talking about the same document, that is - a letter which I signed in the absence of the minister of defence. This is a request to somebody for some equipment under the control of the local staffs to be transferred somewhere. This was not my job, but I did it in the absence of the right person who was supposed to do it. I never knew whether this was at all implemented, nor was it something I was concerned with. And it was not a decision, it was not an order, it was just an accompanying letter with a request of some other body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the letter that the witness is referring to is the letter at tab 4, which is a letter on the head of "Ministry of Economy," dated 24 May 1992, signed by the witness. If the witness could refer to tab 4 and confirm that that is the letter he is referring to, and if I could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that that is an exhibit already. Apologies for that. It's Exhibit P529, tab 176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's at least what your own list says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, is this the document that you were shown when you arrived in The Hague and you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't see it here. When I have it in front of me, then I can tell you -- yes, that is the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So it is the case that in your position of minister of the economy, you did perform tasks which fell within the jurisdiction of other persons in the Republican government.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: No. This was an exception. There was nobody there at the moment to sign the accompanying letter with the request and to give this request some sort of validity. I don't know who this was addressed to. I suppose it was addressed to the Territorial Defence. I don't know whether this was ever implemented. I believe it was the Territorial Defence, because it was them who had at their disposal those obsolete type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you know that Zoran Vitkovic was the commander of the Grbavica Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from Mrs. Plavsic, or any other people at all, or in the media, that there was a criminal who had committed a number of crimes against Muslim civilians specifically, and Croat civilians as well, by the name of Batko?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear it from Plavsic. I'm familiar with the name, it does ring a bell, but I don't know where I heard it. I know that it was somebody's nickname. I don't know whether he was a soldier or police officer or something of the kind. I don't know where I heard it or who from, I just know that it does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question? You just said obsolete weapons. Is that true for the whole of that letter or for -- I mean, what's obsolete on a 60-millimetre mortar? What's obsolete on what is here called a sniper? Is that -- what's obsolete about ammunition 7.62?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking generally about the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence always had old-fashioned equipment and ammunition that they used for various exercises. That's what I am saying. And I believe that there was a position of the government that this should be transferred from unsafe places to somewhat safer places. And I believe that the request of this kind was based on that, and hence the accompanying letter. I really don't know what weapons were old, what weapons were new. I was never interested in that. I never followed that. I suppose that these people could not issue any weapons without some sort of a government's approval. And since I had just joined the government, I never paid too much attention to what this was and whether it was at all important or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just -- you said, as part of your answer -- you don't know whether it was ever implemented: "I believe it was the Territorial Defence, because it was them who had at their disposal those obsolete type of weapons." So it seems that you have a quite clear idea that this letter is about an obsolete type of weapons, which I'm now asking you -- you gave a long answer, but not specifically on my question -- what makes the list here obsolete weapons, the ten items?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know whether the weapons were obsolete. I never saw it. Generally speaking, the Territorial Defence had old-fashioned, obsolete weapons. Whether this was another case of such weapons or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, you drew conclusions as to whom it was addressed. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, in the course of your evidence, you said that you only had one meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, when you -- at the time that you were a minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct that you only had one meeting with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I said that we had our first meeting, and after that, I don't remember whether we had any other meetings. I cannot be sure of that, because I never made a record of whom I met, and when. I was just talking about our first meeting, the meeting when we first were introduced to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: There is material that we have which suggests that you had more meetings with him, possibly not alone but in the presence of Radovan Karadzic. Is that the case, that you did have more meetings in the presence of Radovan Karadzic, or others, with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: What period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At the time that you were a minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also during the time that you were a member of the Ministerial Council of the Assembly of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: It is possible. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in fact, in around February 1992, you met with Karadzic and Krajisnik, and they put a proposal to you about you going to Belgrade, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. And what would have been the purpose of my visit to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At the start of 1992, there were efforts afoot to split the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you one thing? The witness testified this morning, but perhaps I misunderstood it, that he had five to six meetings with Mr. Krajisnik. He said: "No, no, not very often. Perhaps five to six times during my time in office, perhaps not even that often," and then we had a large line of -- we had questions on what he discussed with Mr. Krajisnik. So I have some difficulties in understanding, unless if you say "at the time you were a minister." But I understood this to be during his term of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I hope I haven't misspoken, but there are two terms of office as a minister; his term of office as a minister in the Bosnia and Herzegovina government and his term of office as a minister in the Republika Srpska government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I may have missed that point. Let me just check. Yes, you're right. I made a mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And another matter I did refer to in my question which hasn't been a subject of his evidence today was that he was a member of the Ministerial Council, which the Court has received evidence on that in the form of the minutes of the Ministerial Council. And that, too, was prior to his appointment as a minister for Republika Srpska. Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So possibly if we could continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You'd rather not stop. I do understand. The Defence remained well within the time limits. The witness was scheduled, I think, for four hours, and the time taken -- I have to check that exactly. Approximately three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'd originally estimated, just from memory, it was three or three and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I very recently upped the estimate, but then found, as it turned out, that we came really, for practical purposes, very near to the original estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at the binder, Mr. Margetts, I take it that you're aware of what is not a rule but guidance, but is about 60 per cent. Would you please keep that in mind. Mr. Antic, I would like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and you're still about to give. So don't speak with anyone about it. And we'd like to see you back, although tomorrow, not in the morning hours, but in the afternoon. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, at a quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
